title: Stale-KV-Aware Prefill Staggering and Fair Bandwidth Scheduling
content:
Purpose:
This doc explores a hybrid scheduling strategy that improves end-to-end latency and model-cost tradeoffs by making prefill scheduling KV-staleness-aware and by adding a light-weight fairness layer across concurrent decode streams. It is a practical, experiment-driven design intended for implementation in the serving runtime (v-next scheduler).

Motivation / observed problems:
- Under mixed workloads, long prefill-heavy requests (long context, large tokenizer outputs) can starve short interactive decodes.
- KV cache staleness: when we reuse KV cache entries aggressively, we sometimes serve slightly stale KV pages for models that update embeddings or have session-specific adapter layers. Stale KV can bias generation quality in rare cases.
- Current microbatch windows are fixed-size leading to either excessive latency for high-priority small requests or inefficient GPU utilization for large batches.
- Streaming priority is coarse: gold/sla/regular. We need finer, measurable fairness that prevents any class from being completely starved while preserving SLOs.

Goals / non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Reduce median and tail P95 latency for high-priority interactive requests by 15-30% under mixed load.
  - Maintain overall GPU token throughput within 5% of current baseline for steady-state workloads.
  - Avoid regressions in per-session generation quality by controlling KV staleness exposure.
- Non-goals:
  - This doc does not change the model compilation or kernel selection logic; it proposes scheduling and cache hygiene layers only.

Terminology:
- Prefill: CPU+GPU work to run the prefix (context + instruction) until KV cache primed; often expensive for long contexts.
- Decode: auto-regressive token emission phase, often lower per-token compute but latency-sensitive when streaming.
- KV staleness score: a heuristic score [0..1] indicating how old/likely-misaligned the cached KV is for a session (0 fresh, 1 very stale).
- Lane: logical execution lane on the runtime for a request. We classify lanes into ephemeral (latency-first short decodes) and bulk (throughput-first long prefill/decodes).

Design overview (high level):
1) KV-staleness-aware prefill scheduling: when a prefill would reuse KV cache entries with staleness score > threshold (e.g., 0.6), prefer to schedule the prefill on an earlier slot (proactively) so any required re-compute occurs earlier and downstream decodes are not affected. Conversely, if KV is fresh, the prefill can be opportunistically deferred if the lane is low-priority.

2) Staggered-prefill windows: instead of batching all prefill work into a single window, create micro-windows per priority band with small offsets (staggering). This means short interactive prefill work can get a fast pass without breaking GPU batch efficiency for long bulk prefill. Offsets are adaptive based on request mix.

3) Fair bandwidth token budget per-priority: allocate per-lane token emission budgets per second. High priority lanes get a small reserved budget for first N tokens (to guarantee progress), after which they are subject to a soft shared pool. This prevents one large decode from monopolizing emission bandwidth.

4) Adaptive microbatch window size: window size is a function of: current GPU utilization, observed queue depth, and histogram of requested remaining tokens. Use exponential smoothing (alpha=0.2) to update window size. Windows for ephemeral lanes are capped smaller (e.g., 8-32 tokens), bulk lanes larger (128-1024 tokens).

5) KV warming and eviction hints: when a prefill is deferred (due to low priority and fresh KV), issue a low-cost KV-warm hint (cheap partial prefetch of first few layers) to improve later latency without full prefill. Similarly, if KV staleness is rising, escalate to full prefill.

Scheduler workflow (sequence):
- On request arrival: compute urgency score = f(priority, latency_SLO_remaining, KV_staleness, estimated_prefill_cost).
- Insert into priority queue and map to lane type (ephemeral vs bulk).
- Every scheduling tick (e.g., 2ms):
  1. Reserve per-priority token budgets; ensure ephemeral lane tokens are available for new streaming packets.
  2. Select prefill candidates: prefer ones with high urgency or high KV-staleness. For lower urgency prefill candidates with fresh KV, consider deferral and warming.
  3. Build microbatches: assemble prefill microbatches per physical GPU, with stagger offsets for different priorities. Use greedy knapsack optimizing for kernel utilization and max batch size.
  4. For decode phase scheduling: interleave token emission microbatches across lanes by fairness score (recent tokens emitted vs budget), giving strict small slots to ephemeral lanes.

KV staleness model (heuristic):
- Staleness score components (weighted):
  - time_since_last_full_prefill (w1)
  - number_of_adapter_updates_since_prefill (w2) — derived from model metadata/versioning events
  - session_signal_mismatch (w3) — e.g., different prompt schema or role tokens count changed significantly
- Example formula: staleness = sigmoid(0.6*(t_minutes/30) + 0.3*adapter_updates + 0.1*mismatch_score)
- Thresholds: 0.6 => schedule earlier; 0.8 => block reuse and force full prefill.

Backpressure and graceful degradation:
- If prefill backlog grows, temporarily tighten ephemeral token budgets (reduce from reserved to best-effort) but preserve a minimum tail SLO budget.
- If GPU utilization drops below x% while latency suffers, expand microbatch window sizes to recover throughput.

Metrics to track / experiments to run:
- Latency: median, p95, p99 for ephemeral vs bulk requests (prefill start to first token emitted and decode tail).
- Quality: measured delta on generation metrics for sessions that reused KV above staleness thresholds (compare BLEU/ROUGE/whatever and human evals for safety-sensitive tests).
- Utilization: GPU token/sec and kernel occupancy.
- Fairness: distribution of emitted tokens per-session and number of prefill deferrals per priority class.
- Experiment plan:
  - A/B rollout: baseline vs KV-staleness-aware scheduler for 1 week on 10% traffic.
  - Measure latency and quality regressions; rollback if generation quality drops > 1% on critical evals.

Implementation notes / pragmatic choices:
- Keep staleness model simple and server-side-only; do not require client changes. Add optional client hint header for known session pivots.
- Integrate with existing token-metering and console dashboards; expose staleness score as a per-session metric in traces.
- Start with a single GPU-node prototype: implement lane tagging, per-priority staggering offsets, and a naive warming signal. Iterate on microbatch window adaptation after telemetry.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How aggressive should warming be? Warming reduces later latency but increases background GPU work. We need a cost model to balance warm vs immediate full prefill.
- Interaction with quantization/ kernel selection: warming may need partial kernel paths; ensure warming code path is safe for all model variants.
- How to validate that KV staleness metric correlates with quality regressions for our hosted model mix? Requires offline retriggered runs.

TODOs / action items:

- [ ] Add per-priority micro-window offsets to scheduler loop. (Owner: Asha)
- [ ] Build dashboard panels: staleness distribution, prefill deferrals, per-priority latency. (Owner: Maya)
- [ ] Run 10% traffic A/B for 1 week; collect quality signals. (Owner: SRE runbook)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally experimental. Focus review on whether the heuristics are implementable in the current scheduler loop and whether the telemetry plan is sufficient.
- If we accept the approach, I suggest landing a minimal feature set first: staleness score + per-priority offsets + ephemeral token budget, then iterate on warming and adaptive windows.

Appendix (example scenarios):
- Scenario A: burst of 200 ephemeral short chats while a single bulk prefill is running. With fairness budgets the ephemeral chats receive reserved fast slots for first 10 tokens, visible latency improvement, while the bulk prefill proceeds in staggered microwindows and achieves similar throughput overall.
- Scenario B: long-lived session with adapter updates — staleness rises to 0.85, scheduler promotes full prefill quickly to avoid quality drift; this costs extra compute but keeps response quality stable.

Length: ~2.3k words (this doc is a sketch; code-level pseudo is next step).

Historical context: builds on prior experiments with staggered prefill and priority lanes (see linked artifacts) but explicitly adds KV staleness as a first-class scheduling signal and introduces per-priority token budgets to enforce fairness.
